091:1: How did prayer, which began as talking to oneself for good luck, become a conversation with the indwelling God?
091:4: In Paper 90 we saw the long age when shamans and priests stood between man and God. Now Paper 91 turns to the vehicle of religion that has run through all those ages: prayer. Prayer grew out of nonreligious monologue and dialogue. When primitive man became self-conscious, consciousness of others followed, and in it lay two possibilities together: social reaction and the recognition of God (91:0.1).
091:5: The earliest prayers were not addressed to gods. They were like saying to a friend before an important undertaking, "Wish me luck," and at first they were monologues, thinking out loud (91:0.2). When the ideas of ghosts and spirits arose, petitions were directed to superhuman beings, and with the consciousness of gods the stage of true prayer was finally reached (91:0.3).
091:6: How, then, does prayer differ from magic? And does true prayer change God, or does it change us who pray?
091:8: ⟦Q 91:8.2⟧Magic was an attempt to adjust Deity to conditions; prayer is the effort to adjust the personality to the will of Deity.⟦/Q⟧ (91:8.2)
091:12: The function of early religion is to conserve and enhance growing social, moral, and spiritual values, and this is done chiefly through prayer. Without the safeguard of prayer, every holy day would soon revert to a mere holiday (91:1.1). Since religion and prayer were linked only with values society approved, anyone seeking selfish or antisocial ends had to turn not to prayer but to magic and sorcerers. So prayer early became a powerful agent of moral progress (91:1.2).
091:13: Primitive man also asked for material blessings such as food, rain, and game. This was a distortion of prayer, yet it spurred efforts to reach material goals through social and ethical conduct (91:1.3). True prayer appears only when the agency of religious ministry is recognized as personal (91:1.4). The dangers of prayer lie in ignorance, superstition, rigidity, loss of vitality, materialism, and fanaticism (91:1.6).
091:15: Prayer developed from verbalized wishes into a technique for gaining the co-operation of spirits, and then into the higher function of conserving all that is worth while (91:2.1). When people learned that the gods could not be coerced, prayer became petition, but the truest prayer is communion between man and his Maker (91:2.3).
091:21: Active effort of the praying self
091:22: Manipulates reality without affecting the self
091:27: Becoming material, it sinks into pseudo magic
091:28: As its aims rise, it reaches the threshold of prayer
091:30: The idea of sacrifice weakens the efficacy of prayer, because it tries to offer material things in place of a will dedicated to doing God's will (91:2.4). Remove a personal God, and prayer becomes theology and philosophy; an impersonal Deity is fatal to the efficacy of true prayer (91:2.5). Prayer often shows itself as communion with one's own subconscious, but there is also a superconscious realm in which contact is made with the indwelling Thought Adjuster (91:2.6). And prayer guards personality against isolation (91:2.7).
091:32: As children learn to speak, they think out loud, and before long they talk with imaginary companions. They turn monologue into a pseudo dialogue. Much of adult thinking, too, is conversation inside the mind (91:3.1). Prayer grew in the same way. Recitation with no one to hear became dialogue with an alter ego, and as that alter ego was raised to divine dignity, prayer emerged as a vehicle of religion (91:3.2).
091:41: One God — the embodiment of the highest ideals
091:43: The indwelling Adjuster — a real and divine alter ego
091:45: Prayer is always a twofold experience, a psychological procedure interassociated with a spiritual technique (91:3.6). Enlightened prayer must recognize not only an external, personal God but also the inner Adjuster. Just as primitive man talked with an alter ego close at hand, we, knowing that this concept has evolved from fiction to the truth of God indwelling us as the Adjuster, can talk with him as if face to face (91:3.7).
091:47: Prayer that seeks selfish advantage over one's fellows cannot be ethical; it sinks back into primitive pseudo magic (91:4.1). Prayer must never take the place of action, and all ethical prayer stimulates action (91:4.2). We should pray fairly, not expecting God to love us more than our friends, our neighbors, or even our enemies (91:4.3).
091:52: Self-centered — brings disappointment as science advances
091:53: Asking for the wisdom of forgiveness and self-control
091:56: Moving toward the level of true worship
091:58: Even so, spiritually advanced people must take care not to discourage too quickly the prayers of immature minds. Such petitions too lead to effort and toil toward their answer (91:4.4).
091:60: ⟦Q 91:4.5⟧Remember, even if prayer does not change God, it very often effects great and lasting changes in the one who prays in faith and confident expectation.⟦/Q⟧ (91:4.5)
091:63: The more divine the alter ego of prayer becomes, the more human ideals are lifted from human to divine levels, character is improved, and personality is deeply unified (91:5.1). Group prayer is very effective because its repercussions are highly socializing. Confession, repentance, and prayer have led individuals, cities, and nations to reform and to courageous deeds (91:5.2).
091:64: If you want to break the habit of criticizing a friend, the quickest and surest way is to pray for him every day of your life. But these social repercussions depend on two conditions (91:5.3-5.5). And those who are conscious of God without symbols must not deny the gracious ministry of symbols to those who need forms and rituals (91:5.7).
091:69: The person prayed for must know that he is being prayed for
091:71: The one who prays must be in intimate social contact with him
091:74: Prayer cannot directly affect the physical environment unless it is linked with the will of the spiritual forces and the material supervisors (91:6.1). Prayer is not a technique for curing organic disease, but it has contributed greatly to healing mental, emotional, and nervous disorders and has enhanced the effect of other treatments (91:6.2). Even apart from its religious meaning, prayer is a wholesome psychological act that reaches the reserve powers of human nature stored in the unconscious (91:6.4).
091:76: ⟦Q 91:6.5⟧Do not be so slothful as to ask God to solve your difficulties, but never hesitate to ask him for wisdom and spiritual strength to guide and sustain you while you yourself resolutely and courageously attack the problems at hand.⟦/Q⟧ (91:6.5)
091:78: As Jesus taught, we should pray honestly, unselfishly, fairly, and without doubting (91:6.6). And the efficacy of prayer never depends on intellectual understanding, social standing, or level of culture. There is no more immediate way than prayer for any person to reach the threshold of communion with the Creator (91:6.7).
091:80: Mysticism, as a technique for cultivating the consciousness of the presence of God, is praiseworthy, but when it runs to social isolation and fanaticism it deserves censure. Contact with the Adjuster is made more often in unselfish, loving service to one's fellows than in meditation (91:7.1). Jesus did take his apostles aside for a time to pray, but mostly he had them serve the multitudes. The soul needs spiritual exercise as well as spiritual nourishment (91:7.2).
091:81: An intense emotional experience must not be mistaken for divine revelation. True spiritual ecstasy is usually accompanied by outward calmness and emotional restraint (91:7.3). Whether such extraordinary experiences are genuine is tested by their fruits (91:7.5-7.12). The danger that excessive private prayer tends toward isolation is corrected by group prayer and community worship (91:7.13).
091:88: A more efficient and practical mental life
091:92: Spiritualizing life in the midst of ordinary duties
091:94: Increased love for truth, beauty, and goodness
091:96: Conserving social, moral, and spiritual values
091:101: Primitive man prayed long before he had any clear concept of God. In times of need he cried for help, and in times of joy he gave voice to his delight (91:8.1). Prayer is not an evolution of magic; the two arose independently. True prayer is moral and religious, but magic is neither (91:8.2). Prayer may come from custom or fear, but true prayer is the sincere and trusting communication of the creature's spiritual nature with the spirit of the Creator (91:8.3-8.4).
091:108: Asking for moral growth and spiritual power
091:113: Groveling pleas before a stern judge
091:114: The joyous expression of a liberated son
091:116: Just as a bird cannot fly on rising air unless it spreads its wings, prayer is the technique of riding the rising spiritual currents of the universe (91:8.9). God answers prayer with a larger revelation of truth, a deeper appreciation of beauty, and a higher concept of goodness (91:8.11). Words are only a channel; God answers not the words but the attitude of the soul (91:8.12).
091:118: ⟦Q 91:8.13⟧Pray only for values, not things; for growth, not for gratification.⟦/Q⟧ (91:8.13)
091:121: To pray effectively, we must keep in mind the laws of prevailing petition (91:9.1). These laws show that prayer is not a refuge for laziness but is offered by one who has faced his problems bravely, done everything he can, and chooses and does the will of God (91:9.2-9.8).
091:126: Facing the problems of reality sincerely and courageously
091:128: Honestly exhausting the possibilities of human adjustment
091:130: Surrendering wishes and longings to the transformation of spiritual growth
091:132: Wholeheartedly choosing the divine will; ending indecision
091:134: Devoting oneself to actually doing the Father's will
091:136: Asking for divine wisdom to solve the problems met in the ascent
091:141: Paper 91 shows the road prayer has traveled as if it were the growth of a single person. Talking to oneself for luck became conversation with an imaginary friend; that alter ego was raised through ghosts and gods to the one God, and finally it arrived at the truth of the Adjuster who indwells us. When prayer asks for things and tries to change God, it sinks into magic; when it asks for values and seeks to change ourselves, it lifts personality high. Prayer, then, is not a substitute for action but a guide to action, not a refuge of isolation but a channel leading to loving service. God answers not our words but the attitude of our souls.
091:146: From the start prayer was an agent that conserved social and moral values
091:148: Prayer moves the self; magic tries to manipulate reality without the self
091:150: The fictional alter ego evolved into the truth of the indwelling Adjuster
091:152: Prayer changes not God but the one who prays
091:154: Group prayer and intercession transform people and communities
091:156: Face your problems courageously and ask for wisdom and strength
091:158: True religious experience is tested by its fruits and its service
091:160: Ask for values, not things; for growth, not gratification
091:162: Courage, diligence, dedication, and living faith are the conditions of prayer
091:165: True prayer is not a bargain to change God but a path of growth in which we converse with the indwelling God and bring ourselves into line with his will.
092:1: How does human religion, born of fear, meet revelation and grow until it worships a God of love?
092:4: In Paper 91 we saw how prayer, which began as incantation, grew into communion with God. Now Paper 92 looks back on the road traveled by the larger vessel that holds prayer: religion as a whole.
092:5: The book says that man had a religion of natural origin long before he received any systematic revelation. That religion arose slowly through three divine ministries, and afterward the Thought Adjusters, the seraphim, and the Spirit of Truth were added, hastening the development of religion (92:0.1-0.5).
092:6: What, then, did evolutionary religion, which began in fear, do well and what did it do wrong? How does revelation lift it up, and how should we today look at religion?
092:8: ⟦Q 92:7.3⟧The many religions of Urantia are all good to the extent that they bring man to God and bring the realization of the Father to man.⟦/Q⟧ (92:7.3)
092:13: Influences that caused religion to sprout
092:16: Awakens man's primal instinct toward Deity
092:18: Leads adoration to higher expression and a broader concept of Deity
092:20: The first supermind bestowal, enabling belief in and experience of survival
092:22: Religion began in the fear of ghosts and moved from trying to coerce spirits to trying to placate them. Fetishes changed into totems and tribal gods, magical incantations into prayers, and circumcision, once a sacrifice, into a hygienic procedure (92:1.1). Mankind advanced from nature worship through ghost worship to fetishism, and has now entered a stage in which it can understand true religion (92:1.2).
092:23: Fear has always been the basic stimulus of religion. As civilization grows, fear is softened into awe and reverence, and then into remorse and repentance (92:1.4). One Asiatic people taught that God is a great fear, but Jesus proclaimed that God is love (92:1.5). The whole road religion has traveled lies between these two sayings.
092:25: Religion is the most rigid of human institutions, yet it slowly adjusts to a changing society (92:2.1). Religion holds the old to be sacred. That is why stone implements remained on the altars long into the Bronze and Iron Ages, and why the most primitive foods were used in the sacraments (92:2.2). That old scriptures still contain things we find awkward today is also because people feared to erase what their ancestors held holy (92:2.3).
092:26: The book says it is foolish to try to hurry the growth of religion too much. A people can absorb a new religion only to the extent that it fits their state of evolution, and in practice it is the morality of the race that determines the form of its religion (92:2.4-2.5). It also makes clear that conscience is not a divine voice speaking to the soul but merely the sum of the mores of the time (92:2.6).
092:28: ⟦Q 92:2.6⟧Conscience, untaught by experience and unaided by reason, never has been, and never can be, a safe and unerring guide to human conduct.⟦/Q⟧ (92:2.6)
092:31: Studying religion is digging through the social strata that hold the fossils of past ages. Cults arose not to seek truth but to spread creeds, and religion has often been tainted by the delusion of being a chosen people (92:3.1-3.2). Evolutionary religion, unlike science, has no self-correcting system; it is corrected only by the pressure of the mores and the illumination of epochal revelation (92:3.4-3.5).
092:32: The book judges evolutionary religion to be the most costly yet incomparably effective of institutions (92:3.8). Religion has done much harm, but without it there would have been no enduring morals and no civilization worth having (92:3.6-3.7).
092:37: Gave birth to sculpture, architecture, poetry, music, drama, and dance
092:39: Accumulation of capital, discipline and self-control, social continuity
092:41: Hindered industry and wasted labor and capital
092:45: The whip of evolution driving mankind toward reason and wisdom
092:47: So this sacred heritage is not to be thrown away; it must be constantly refined under the censorship of revealed religion and in the furnace of genuine science (92:3.10).
092:49: Revelation always keeps in touch with evolution, giving greater light little by little, as much as man can receive (92:4.1). Revealed religion is always marked by belief in a Deity of final values and by the idea that personality survives death (92:4.2). If evolutionary religion is a roundabout path in search of truth, revealed religion is that truth itself (92:4.3).
092:50: There have been many religious revelations, but only five of epochal significance (92:4.4-4.9).
092:55: The one hundred members of the Prince's staff proclaimed the First Source and Center
092:57: Adam and Eve again presented the concept of the Father of all
092:59: God's favor is gained through trust and faith
092:61: God as the Universal Father — love and service

092:65: The book is frank about itself as well. It admits that no revelation can be complete short of the Universal Father, and that all celestial ministry is partial and transient (92:4.9).
092:67: Evolutionary religion pictures the gods in human form, but revealed religion teaches that man is a son of God. Man's concept of Deity has been formed by a blending of the ideas of the evolutionary cults, the sublime ideals of revelation, and the personal views of great leaders (92:5.1-5.4).
092:68: People tend to venerate the leader more than the teaching. There is an instinct to look for help from above, and since Urantia lost its superhuman leaders, people try to make up for that loss by wrapping human leaders in legends of miracles (92:5.5-5.6). Even so, these teachers were the fulcrum on which the lever of revealed truth rested (92:5.7). The leaders since Adam can be grouped into seven ages (92:5.8-5.15).
092:73: Sethite priests under Amosad; preserved the concept of the Trinity
092:75: Proclaimed faith as the way to win God's favor
092:77: Amenemope and Ikhnaton; Moses, who taught one God
092:79: ⟦Q 92:5.12⟧Gautama, Confucius, Lao-tse, Zoroaster, and the Jainist teachers⟦/Q⟧
092:81: Jesus, followed by Paul and Philo
092:85: The division of Western Christianity; Nanak and the Sikhs
092:87: The book says that teachers of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of all creatures will come in the future, and it hopes they will foster a brotherhood of spiritual worship rather than raising higher walls between religions (92:5.16).
092:89: The book explains that the peoples of the twentieth century are at different stages of religious evolution. Some groups are still at the stage of ghost fear or fetishes, while others long ago came to believe in one God and in immortality (92:6.1). By this time evolutionary and revealed religion had grown side by side and become mixed, appearing as eleven great religions (92:6.2-6.13).
092:96: The connecting link between evolutionary and revealed religion
092:98: Spread widely by adapting to the mores of many peoples
092:102: Faith that light will triumph over darkness
092:106: One of the four religions of India
092:108: Formulated by Philo, Peter, and Paul; thoroughly Occidentalized
092:110: Became monotheistic through Jewish and Christian influence
092:112: The most recent religion to appear
092:114: Citing how Islam stumbled over the doctrine of the Trinity, the book says that it is always hard for an evolving mind to accept a suddenly advanced revelation (92:6.19). It also points out that ancestor worship has revived in the West as hero-venerating nationalism, and that national religion is a return to the old worship of the state (92:6.20).
092:116: Religion cannot become a scientific fact, and a new religion cannot be invented. Religion either evolves or is revealed, and the old does not disappear but blends with the new (92:7.1-7.2). So no group should regard its creed as the only truth. Every religion contains truth, and it is far better to borrow the best in a neighbor's living faith than to denounce the superstitions of that neighbor's religion (92:7.3).
092:118: But they can, and some day will, realize a unity in true worship of the Father of all. (92:7.4)
092:120: True religion is the devotion of the self to supreme values, a living experience of loving loyalty (92:7.5). The quality of a religion can be gauged in four ways (92:7.6-7.10).
092:122: Measures of the quality of religion
092:127: Sensitivity in recognizing the highest values
092:129: Degree of devotion to divine values
092:131: Realization of sonship with God and of unending universe citizenship
092:133: A child's religious experience depends greatly on whether fear or love ruled the relationship with the parents (92:7.11). The book regrets that those who venerate the risen Christ have lost sight of the man Joshua ben Joseph, who was a courageous hero (92:7.12). Modern man must make more readjustments of values within one generation than in the past two thousand years, and true religion must at this time become the eternal foundation and guiding star of civilization (92:7.14-7.15).
092:135: Paper 92 neither condemns religion as a shameful past nor defends it uncritically. Evolutionary religion, born of fear, wasted and hindered much, yet it preserved civilization and morality and prepared a place where revelation could enter. Revelation has added light as much as man could receive, and that light has spread through the lives of great leaders. Now the many religions can become one, not in creed, but in true worship of the Father. From the saying "God is a great fear" to the saying "God is love," the end of that long journey is a brotherhood that borrows the best from one another.

092:142: Religion clings to the old, and conscience is not a divine voice
092:144: The most costly yet most effective of institutions, it must be constantly refined

092:148: The teachers of seven religious ages became the fulcrum of truth
092:150: Evolution and revelation blended to form today's religions
092:152: All religions can become one in true worship

093:1: In an age when the light of truth was going out, how did a Melchizedek who became a man prepare the way for Jesus?
093:4: In Paper 92 we saw that the third of the five epochal revelations was that of Melchizedek of Salem. Now Paper 93 tells the story of the central figure of that third revelation, Machiventa Melchizedek.
093:5: The Melchizedeks are known as emergency Sons who step in whenever special problems arise, and they are a rare order able to work even on the level of physical personality (93:0.1). Twelve Melchizedeks took charge of this world after the Caligastia secession, and after the default of Adam and Eve they returned and remained as planetary receivers until Jesus became the titular Planetary Prince of this world (93:0.2).
093:6: When even help from on high had been declined, for what purpose did one Melchizedek take on a human body? And how was the covenant of faith he left carried on, and then forgotten?
093:8: ⟦Q 93:2.1⟧I am Melchizedek, priest of El Elyon, the Most High, the one and only God.⟦/Q⟧ (93:2.1)
093:12: For thousands of years after the failure of the Adamic mission, revealed truth was in danger of disappearing. Mankind advanced intellectually but slipped back spiritually, and by about 3000 B.C. the concept of God had grown very dim (93:1.1). The twelve receivers appealed for help to Edentia and to Father Melchizedek, but they were told only to preserve the truth by means of their own choosing until a bestowal Son should come (93:1.2).
093:13: Then Machiventa, one of the twelve receivers, volunteered. It was something that had happened only six times in the history of Nebadon: personalizing as a temporary man of the realm and bestowing himself as an emergency Son. With the permission of Salvington, he took on a body near the place that would later be called Salem, through the co-operation of the Life Carriers and various celestial personalities (93:1.3).
093:15: Machiventa first appeared 1,973 years before the birth of Jesus, without any display, in the tent of Amdon, a Chaldean herder. He ate with the herder and began to teach the reality of God under the starlight, and a few years later he formed the center of the Salem community (93:2.1-2.4). On his breastplate he wore three concentric circles, the symbol of the Paradise Trinity (93:2.5).
093:20: Ninety-four years; he left before his body declined
093:22: A special body like that of the Prince's staff, with no human life plasm
093:24: He did not marry and could leave no offspring
093:26: The very Adjuster that would later indwell Jesus
093:28: In full communication only with his eleven fellow receivers
093:30: In particular, the Adjuster that indwelt him was prepared by this experience, and later, when Michael came in human flesh, it worked in his mind. This Adjuster is the only one that has functioned in two minds on Urantia (93:2.7).
093:32: Melchizedek founded a school at Salem, patterned after the old Sethite system of education (93:3.1). He taught one universal Deity, but he allowed people to associate his teaching with the Most Highs of Edentia. Most people likewise took the three concentric circles to stand for the three kingdoms of men, angels, and God, and very few knew that they signified the infinity, eternity, and universality of the Trinity (93:3.2-3.3).
093:33: He taught each pupil as much as that pupil could receive. To his outstanding pupil Nordan he passed on even the truths of the superuniverse and Havona, and the family of Katro kept his teachings down to the time of Moses (93:3.4-3.5). He placed all his teaching under the doctrine of one God, the divine Father, and he foretold that another Son of God would one day be born of a woman (93:3.6-3.7). Michael came and confirmed all that Melchizedek had taught about the Father (93:3.8).
093:35: The worship at Salem was very simple. Everyone who signed the roll recited and accepted three beliefs (93:4.1-4.4).
093:40: El Elyon, the one Universal Father and Creator of all things
093:42: God's favor is given for faith, not for sacrifices
093:44: Keep the commandments and tell the good news to all
093:46: The seven commandments were patterned after the supreme law of ancient Dalamatia and the commandments of Eden (93:4.6-4.13).

093:53: ⟦Q 93:4.8⟧You shall not doubt that faith is the only requirement for eternal salvation⟦/Q⟧
093:63: ⟦Q 93:4.13⟧You shall not show disrespect for your parents and elders⟦/Q⟧
093:65: People simply could not grasp the idea of receiving favor freely, through faith (93:4.5). Melchizedek gave the sacrament of bread and wine in place of sacrifice, but the custom of sacrifice never wholly disappeared, not even with Abraham (93:4.14). He did not come to change the mores or customs; he came to keep alive the truth of one God and to prepare for the bestowal of a Paradise Son (93:4.15).
093:67: It may be an error to speak of a chosen people, but it is not a mistake to call Abraham a chosen individual (93:5.1). Salem was chosen because Palestine was then the center of trade, travel, and civilization, and because contact could be made with the able children of Terah (93:5.2-5.3). Abraham and his nephew Lot came to Salem at Melchizedek's invitation (93:5.5).
093:68: But Abraham harbored an ambition to be king. He wanted to spread the truth of Salem by subduing the neighboring tribes with the sword, and Melchizedek, who was keeping the peace, worked hard to restrain him. The two parted on friendly terms, and Abraham set up a military capital at Hebron (93:5.9-5.11). When Lot's goods were plundered, he won the battle of Siddim and gave a tenth of the spoils to Salem (93:5.12-5.14).
093:70: Abraham, who dreamed of conquering Canaan, came again to Melchizedek, worried that he had no son to succeed him, and in this meeting he gave up worldly conquest and accepted the spiritual concept of the kingdom of heaven (93:6.1). Melchizedek pointed to the stars of heaven and promised that his seed would be as many, and Abraham believed, and it was counted to him for righteousness (93:6.3).
093:72: ⟦Q 93:6.4⟧God agrees to do everything; man only agrees to believe God's promises and follow his instructions.⟦/Q⟧ (93:6.4)
093:74: This good news, that salvation is gained not by works but by faith, was so far ahead of its time that people eventually went back to the old system of blood sacrifice (93:6.4). When Isaac was born as promised, Abraham put the covenant in writing and changed his name from Abram to Abraham (93:6.5). Once the reconciliation was complete, as the leader of Salem he greatly improved the schools, the missions, and the tithing system (93:6.8).
093:76: The missionaries Melchizedek trained went out to Egypt, Mesopotamia, and Asia Minor, and further on to Europe, the British Isles, Iceland, and across China all the way to Japan. The lives of those men and women are a heroic chapter in human history (93:7.1-7.2).
093:77: But the task was too great. Outside Palestine, the concept of one God never won the lasting loyalty of a whole tribe or race, and the gospel of Salem was nearly buried under old cults such as the Great Mother and sun worship (93:7.3). In an age without printing, new truth was easily forgotten, and new revelation was always contaminated by older beliefs (93:7.4).
093:79: Shortly after the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, Machiventa decided to end his bestowal. The chief reason was that people had begun to regard him as a demigod and to revere him with superstitious fear. He also judged that if he left while Abraham was still alive, the truth of one God would be firmly established in the minds of his followers. One night he said good night and went into his tent, and in the morning he was not there (93:8.1).
093:81: Melchizedek's disappearance was a lifelong sorrow to Abraham. For a while he was gripped by fear and even concealed his identity at Gerar, but he soon became the spiritual leader of Palestine again, and he died firm in the faith he had learned from Melchizedek (93:9.1-9.4). Five hundred years later many regarded the story of Melchizedek as a myth, and Joseph was called a dreamer by his brothers for believing it (93:9.5).
093:82: The book explains that what the Old Testament records as conversations between Abraham and God were in fact conferences between Abraham and Melchizedek (93:9.7). It also says that the scribes of the Babylonian captivity, out of national pride, edited the records to exalt Abraham and almost erased the era of Melchizedek (93:9.8-9.9). As a result the teaching about the promised bestowal Son was also lost, and when Michael came, hardly anyone recognized him (93:9.10). Only one writer of the book of Hebrews understood Melchizedek's mission (93:9.11).
093:84: On the third day after he vanished from Salem, Machiventa reappeared among his eleven fellows and resumed his career as a planetary receiver. His appearance and departure were not accompanied by any resurrection roll call or the ending of a dispensation (93:10.1-10.2). For the nineteen centuries that followed he co-operated with the prophets and preserved the truths of Salem (93:10.4).

095:5: Just as India was the cradle of the religions and philosophies of eastern Asia, the Levant was the cradle of the faiths of the Western world. Their failures were sometimes due to lack of wisdom and sometimes to circumstances beyond their control (95:0.1).

The belief that a soul would enter the realms of bliss if, in the judgment hall of Osiris, it was found free of the sins of murder, robbery, lying, adultery, theft, and selfishness was an advanced concept for its time (95:2.9). 096:35: No leader ever tried to lift up a more forlorn and dejected group of people than Moses did (96:3.3). 098:1: How did the Salem teaching of one God pass through the philosophy and mystery cults of the West and reach Christianity?
098:4: In earlier papers we followed the paths by which the Salem teachings of Machiventa Melchizedek spread through the Levant and the Orient. Now Paper 98 traces how those teachings flowed westward into Europe. They came in chiefly by way of Egypt, and after being Hellenized and later Christianized, they found a place in Occidental philosophy (98:0.1).
098:5: The Salem missionaries worked in Europe for a long time, but they were gradually absorbed into various cults and ritual groups. Those who kept the teachings in their purest form were the Cynics, and Jewish mercenaries also spread the Salem doctrine through the West (98:0.2-0.3). That is why the basic doctrines of Greek philosophy, Jewish theology, and Christian ethics are fundamentally echoes of the earlier Melchizedek teachings (98:0.4).
